newsitem.title: USA: Tyson Foods lobbyist trial goes to jury.
newsitem.headline: Tyson Foods lobbyist trial goes to jury.

text.p: Federal prosecutors, during closing arguments Friday, flatly accused Tyson Foods Inc lobbyist Jack Williams of lying in an investigation of former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy.
Defense attorney Barry Levine said the charges of making false statements grew from inept and cursory questioning of Williams by investigators who did not keep a verbatim account of their interviews.
If convicted, Williams would face a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.
A predominantly black and female jury heard four days of testimony before final arguments on Friday.
Espy resigned in 1994 amid allegations he improperly accepted gifts from businesses regulated by his department. Independent counsel Donald Smaltz has investigated the matter since late 1994.
Lead prosecutor Robert Ray said Williams, in two sessions with Agriculture Department and FBI agents "spoke words and those words were lies."
"This is a case about the failings of investigators," Levine told jurors. "They want to blame him about questions they did not ask...You can't let that happen."

According to the agents, Williams said he knew nothing about Espy's attendance as a Tyson Foods guest at a January 16, 1994, pro football game in Dallas and never spoke to Espy's girlfriend, Patricia Dempsey, by telephone.

Other witnesses said Williams paid for Dempsey's airline ticket to the game and notified Tyson headquarters to expect her. He also relayed to her by fax an application for a Tyson Foundation scholarship.

While Ray and an assistant, Barry Coburn, said evidence consistently showed that Williams repeatedly misled investigators, Levine said it was impossible to know exactly what Williams was asked and what he said.

Investigators kept imprecise notes with paraphrasings of their interviews, Levine said, and failed to aggressively probe Williams' replies. He pointed to discrepancies in the agents' descriptions of the interviews -- "flyspecking" in Coburn's view that did nothing to weaken the case.
Legal experts have said the outcome of the case might be key in the Espy investigation and its credibility.
A Smaltz spokesman said the Espy investigation would not be affected by the verdict on Williams.
